SeeRuth 3:1, footnotea; see also “Ruth 2:18–20. Why was it significant that Boaz was one of Naomi’s ‘next kinsmen’?” Ruth’s words echoed the words of Boaz from their initial meeting. In that conversation, Boaz said, “The Lord recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the Lord God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust” (Ruth 2:12). Ruth may have been implying that Jehovah would spread His protective wing over her when Boaz spread his wing over her by marrying her (see Holzapfel and others,Jehovah and the World of the Old Testament, 187; Muhlestein, “Ruth, Redemption, Covenant, and Christ,” 200).

The books of 1 and 2 Samuel were originally one book in the Hebrew Bible. They were likely divided into two books when the Bible was translated into Greek (see Holzapfel and others,Jehovah and the World of the Old Testament, 190).

See1 Samuel 3:19–21. President Joseph Fielding Smith taught: “The withdrawal of the higher priesthood was from the people as a body, but the Lord still left among them men holding the Melchizedek Priesthood, with power to officiate in all its ordinances, so far as he determined that these ordinances should be granted unto the people. Therefore Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Ezekiel, Elijah, and others of the prophets held the Melchizedek Priesthood” (Doctrines of Salvation, comp. Bruce R. McConkie [1956], 3:85).

The Old Testament records instances of people from other tribes being authorized by the Lord to offer sacrifices. Examples include Joshua from the tribe of Ephraim (seeNumbers 13:8;Joshua 8:30–31); Gideon from the tribe of Manasseh (seeJudges 6:15, 25–28); and David from the tribe of Judah (see2 Samuel 6:17–18;24:25;Matthew 1:1–6). Samuel’s lineage is unclear; he and his father, Elkanah, are listed in the Levite genealogy recorded in1 Chronicles 6:27–28.
